breakfast.name: Ħobż biż-Żejt (Bread with Tomato and Oil)
instructions: Slice open ftira bread
Spread with kunserva
Drizzle olive oil generously
Top with capers, olives, tuna, onion
breakfast.description: Maltese bread rubbed with tomato paste and olive oil — the quintessential snack.

breakfast.name: Pastizzi
instructions: Make flaky pastry dough
Fill with ricotta or pea mixture
Shape into diamond pastizzi
Brush with egg
Bake at 200°C 25 min
breakfast.description: Flaky diamond-shaped pastries — ricotta or pea filled — Malta's icon.

breakfast.name: Ftira (Maltese Ring Bread)
instructions: Mix flour, yeast, water, salt, olive oil into a dough
Knead until smooth and elastic — the olive oil enriches the crumb
Let rise 1 hour
Shape into a ring — the ring shape is the signature of Maltese ftira
The ring allows even baking — no dense center
Let rise again 30 minutes
Bake at 220°C until golden with a hollow-sounding crust
The crust should be firm; the crumb airy and slightly chewy
Ftira is Malta's ancient bread — distinct from regular round loaves
The ring shape is specific to Malta and related to the ancient Mediterranean bread tradition
Used for sandwiches (ftira tal-bahar — tuna sandwich) or eaten with oil
breakfast.description: Malta's ring-shaped bread — yeasted dough enriched with olive oil, shaped into a ring (which allows even baking), baked until golden. The ring shape is specifically Maltese, connected to ancient Mediterranean bread traditions. Used for Malta's famous tuna sandwiches (ftira tal-bahar) or eaten simply with olive oil.

breakfast.name: Kunserva (Tomato Paste) on Bread
ingredients: Kunserva (concentrated sun-dried tomato paste — thick, sweet, intense)
instructions: Kunserva is Malta's sun-dried tomato paste — concentrated by sun-drying over days
The result is much thicker and sweeter than Italian tomato paste
Spread kunserva generously on fresh bread
Drizzle with olive oil
Salt
That's it — no additions needed
Kunserva on bread (hobz biz-zejt) is Malta's simplest and most beloved breakfast
The concentrated tomato sweetness against good olive oil on fresh bread
The kunserva's sweetness comes from the concentrated sun-drying, not added sugar
Malta's summer sun does the work — the concentrated tomato is solar energy made edible
breakfast.description: Malta's simplest breakfast — thickly spread kunserva (Malta's sun-dried concentrated tomato paste, much sweeter and thicker than Italian equivalent) on fresh bread with olive oil. The tomato's natural sugars concentrate through sun-drying into an intensely sweet paste. Kunserva on bread is Malta's most iconic food moment: sun, tomatoes, oil, bread.

lunch.name: Stuffat tal-Fenek (Rabbit Stew)
instructions: Marinate rabbit in wine overnight
Brown rabbit pieces
Sauté onions, garlic
Add wine, tomatoes, herbs
Simmer 2 hours until tender
Serve with spaghetti
lunch.description: Malta's national dish — slow-braised rabbit in red wine.

lunch.name: Bragioli (Beef Olives)
ingredients: Filling: breadcrumbs, bacon, egg, parsley, garlic
instructions: Pound beef thin, fill and roll, tie
Brown the rolls
Make tomato-wine sauce
Braise rolls in sauce 90 min
Add peas near end
lunch.description: Stuffed rolled beef in tomato-wine sauce.

lunch.name: Imqarrun il-Forn (Baked Macaroni)
instructions: Boil macaroni until just underdone — it finishes in the oven
Make meat sauce: fry onion, garlic, add minced pork-beef, brown well
Add tomato, wine, bay leaf, herbs — simmer 20 minutes
Mix cooked macaroni with meat sauce
The distinguishing Maltese step: beat eggs, mix into the pasta before baking
The eggs bind the pasta into a layered cake-like structure when baked
Transfer to a baking dish, top with cheese
Bake until the top is golden and the egg has set
The result slices like a cake — firm enough to cut into squares
Imqarrun il-forn (baked macaroni) is Malta's Sunday dish
The Italian pasta influence transformed through the Maltese baked-egg technique
lunch.description: Malta's Sunday pasta cake — macaroni mixed with pork-beef meat sauce and beaten eggs, baked until the egg sets into a firm, sliceable cake topped with golden cheese. The egg-binding technique (transforming pasta into a cuttable cake) is distinctly Maltese. Italian pasta arrived via Sicily and Arab traders; the Maltese baked it with eggs and made it their own.

lunch.name: Gbejniet (Maltese Cheeselets)
ingredients: Gbejniet (small Maltese fresh sheep or goat cheeses — the fresh white variety)
instructions: Gbejniet are Malta's unique small round cheeses — made from sheep or goat milk
The fresh variety is mild, slightly tangy, and soft — similar to fresh ricotta in texture but firmer
The peppered/dried variety (imsaħħna) is air-dried with black pepper coating
Serve fresh gbejniet with drizzled olive oil and cracked black pepper
Accompanied by bread and kunserva
Gbejniet are Malta's contribution to Mediterranean cheese culture
The small, round shape is specific — each one is palm-sized
GI-protected: authentic gbejniet must come from Malta or Gozo
The dried, peppered gbejniet has a sharp, concentrated sheep milk flavor
Both varieties are eaten at every Maltese meal
lunch.description: Malta's unique cheese — small round fresh sheep or goat milk cheeses (gbejniet), eaten fresh with olive oil and black pepper or dried with a black pepper coating (imsaħħna). GI-protected to Malta and Gozo. The fresh version is mild and soft; the dried version is sharp and concentrated. Gbejniet appear at every Maltese table.

dinner.name: Lampuki Pie (Fish Pie)
instructions: Line dish with pastry
Layer fish with vegetables, olives, capers
Cover with pastry, seal
Bake at 180°C 40 min
dinner.description: Traditional fish pie with dolphinfish, vegetables, and capers.

dinner.name: Aljotta (Fish Soup)
instructions: Sauté garlic and onion
Add tomatoes, fish, herbs, water
Simmer 20 min
Remove fish, flake, return
Add rice, cook until done
Finish with lemon and mint
dinner.description: Garlicky Maltese fish soup with marjoram and mint.

dinner.name: Kapunata (Maltese Caponata)
instructions: Cube all vegetables, salt eggplant briefly to draw moisture
Fry each vegetable separately in olive oil — then combine
The Maltese version differs from Sicilian caponata in being less sweet
Add tomato, olives, capers
Add vinegar and a small amount of sugar — the agrodolce balance
Simmer until combined and saucy
Finish with fresh basil
Kapunata is Malta's summer vegetable preserve — the olive oil protects it
Kept in a jar with oil, it lasts weeks and improves
The Maltese influence from Sicily is clear but the Maltese have their own balance
Served as a side, a spread on bread, or alongside fish and meat
dinner.description: Malta's sweet-sour vegetable preserve — eggplant, zucchini, and peppers fried separately then combined with tomato, olives, capers, and vinegar-sugar (less sweet than Sicilian caponata). Cooked in generous olive oil and kept submerged under oil, kapunata lasts weeks and improves. Malta's most important summer preserve.

dinner.name: Qarnit (Octopus in Red Wine)
ingredients: Red wine (generous — enough to almost submerge)
instructions: The Maltese octopus technique: no added water
Octopus releases its own liquid as it cooks
Brown onion and garlic in olive oil in a heavy pot
Add octopus pieces
Pour wine generously — the wine braising liquid is the sauce
Add bay leaf, cloves, black pepper
Low heat, covered, 50-60 minutes — the octopus tenderizes in the wine
The wine and octopus liquid reduce into a rich, deep purple-red braising sauce
The octopus should be fork-tender with no rubbery resistance
Qarnit (octopus) is Malta's most celebrated seafood dish
The Mediterranean octopus, dried on lines in the sun (traditional) before cooking, is considered superior
dinner.description: Malta's octopus in red wine — whole octopus braised in generous red wine with no added water (the octopus provides its own liquid), cooked until fork-tender in a purple-red sauce. Traditional dried octopus (hung on lines in the sun first) is considered superior in flavor. The no-water technique concentrates the wine and octopus flavors.

dinner.name: Bragioli (Beef Olives)
ingredients: Breadcrumb stuffing: stale bread, egg, garlic, parsley, bacon, Parmesan
instructions: Pound beef slices thin
Make stuffing: soak stale bread in water, squeeze dry, mix with egg, garlic, parsley, chopped bacon, Parmesan
Place stuffing on each beef slice
Roll tightly, secure with toothpick or kitchen string
Brown rolled beef olives in olive oil on all sides
Add tomato sauce, red wine — enough to half-submerge
Braise on low heat 45-55 minutes
The beef becomes tender; the sauce reduces and concentrates
Bragioli (beef olives — no actual olives) is Malta's celebration dinner
The stuffed rolled beef in wine sauce is Maltese but clearly shows the Italian-Sicilian influence
A Sunday and Christmas dish — time-consuming to prepare
dinner.description: Malta's stuffed beef roll — thin beef slices wrapped around a breadcrumb, bacon, and Parmesan stuffing, braised in tomato-wine sauce. The Sicilian influence is unmistakable (the same technique as involtini) but the Maltese stuffing version is their own. Called 'beef olives' despite containing no olives — a British naming convention that somehow crossed to Malta.

snacks.name: Bigilla (Bean Dip)
instructions: Boil beans until very soft
Mash with garlic, olive oil, chili
Add mint and parsley
Serve with bread or crackers

snacks.name: Ħobż biż-Żejt (Bread with Oil and Tomato)
instructions: This is Malta's national sandwich — and it's barely a recipe
Tear or slice bread
Rub with kunserva — or spread generously
Pour olive oil
Add whatever you have: capers, olives, tuna, gbejniet, fresh tomato
The combinations are personal and regional
Ħobż biż-żejt is what every Maltese child grew up eating
It's eaten at the beach, on fishing boats, at work
The quality of the bread and the kunserva makes it
Nothing else in Maltese food culture is as universally beloved
The simplicity IS the recipe — good ingredients, no fuss
snacks.description: Malta's national snack — bread rubbed or spread with kunserva (concentrated tomato paste), drizzled with olive oil, and topped with whatever is at hand: capers, olives, tuna, or gbejniet. Every Maltese person grew up with this. The simplicity is the point. Beach food, boat food, childhood food. The quality of the bread and the kunserva intensity is everything.

snacks.name: Ftira Sandwich (Tuna Ftira)
instructions: Split the ftira ring horizontally
Spread kunserva on the inside
Fill with tuna, sliced tomato, onion rings, olives, capers
Drizzle with the olive oil from the tuna tin
Optional: add gbejniet (cheese), anchovies
The ftira sandwich is Malta's street food lunch
The ring shape creates a thick sandwich that holds generous fillings
The tuna-kunserva-caper combination is the classic filling
Every Maltese knows their preferred combination — there are passionate opinions
The ftira sandwich is also called 'Maltese pizza' outside Malta (incorrectly — it's a sandwich)
snacks.description: Malta's tuna ring sandwich — ftira bread split and filled with tuna, tomato, olives, capers, and kunserva. The ring shape creates a robust, holdable sandwich for beach days, boat trips, and work lunches. The tuna-kunserva-caper combination is the classic. Every Maltese has a precise opinion on the correct filling ratio.

snacks.name: Prinjolata (Pine Nut Carnival Cake)
instructions: Make a light sponge cake and crumble it
Mix crumbled sponge with whipped cream, pine nuts, lemon zest, vanilla
Mold into a dome shape — pressing firmly
The dome shape is the prinjolata's signature
Refrigerate until firm
Decorate exterior with chocolate drizzle, halved cherries, pine nuts
The prinjolata is Malta's carnival dessert — made for Carnival season (pre-Lent)
The dome shape mirrors the Maltese baroque architectural domes
Pine nuts and cherries are the Maltese pastry signature from Arab influence
The prinjolata appears only during Carnival — its seasonal rarity makes it precious
snacks.description: Malta's carnival dome cake — crumbled sponge mixed with whipped cream, pine nuts, and lemon zest, molded into a dome, and decorated with chocolate, cherries, and pine nuts. Served only during Carnival season (pre-Lent). The dome shape mirrors Malta's famous baroque church domes. The pine nut and cherry combination traces to Arab-Sicilian pastry influence on the islands.

desserts.name: Imqaret (Date Diamonds)
ingredients: Filling: dates, orange peel, anise, cloves
instructions: Cook date filling with spices
Make pastry, fill, cut diamonds
Deep fry until golden
Drizzle with honey
desserts.description: Fried date-filled pastry diamonds drizzled with honey.

desserts.name: Qaghaq tal-Għasel (Honey Rings)
ingredients: Pastry dough (flour, lard, water — traditional short pastry)
Honey filling: honey, candied peel, anise, cocoa, carob syrup, sesame
instructions: Make short pastry with flour and lard — traditional Maltese pastry uses lard
Prepare honey filling: mix honey with candied citrus peel, anise, cocoa, carob syrup, sesame seeds
The filling is very complex — many components
Pipe filling into a pastry tube, seal the edges
Shape into a ring
Bake until lightly golden
The ring shape means the honey filling is inside the complete pastry loop
Qaghaq tal-għasel is Malta's ancient Christmas pastry
The Arabic-influenced filling (honey, anise, sesame) reflects Arab rule of Malta 870-1091 CE
The rings are exchanged as gifts at Christmas
Every Maltese family has their specific honey ring recipe — closely guarded
desserts.description: Malta's Christmas honey ring — short pastry filled with a complex honey-anise-cocoa-carob-sesame filling, baked into a ring. The filling reflects Arab rule of Malta (870-1091 CE): honey, anise, sesame, and citrus are all Arab pastry elements. Exchanged as Christmas gifts. Every family's specific honey filling recipe is a closely guarded secret.

desserts.name: Kannoli tal-Irkotta (Ricotta Pastry)
ingredients: Pastry shell: flour, lard, Marsala wine
Ricotta filling: sheep's milk ricotta, sugar, dark chocolate chips, candied orange peel
instructions: Make the pastry dough with flour, lard, Marsala wine — the wine adds complexity
Roll and cut into circles
Roll around metal forms (or improvise with dowels)
Fry the rolled pastry until golden and crispy — they puff and blister
Cool on the forms, then slide off
Maltese kannoli come directly from Sicily — the Arab-influenced fried pastry
But the Maltese filling uses sheep's ricotta (not cow's) — milder, creamier
Fill just before serving — the pastry softens quickly in contact with the ricotta
The chocolate chip and candied orange peel are traditional additions
The Sicilian-Maltese cultural exchange in pastry: which came first, Malta or Sicily?
desserts.description: Malta's sicilian-inherited fried pastry — fried pastry tubes filled with sweetened sheep's milk ricotta, chocolate chips, and candied orange peel. Malta's shared history with Sicily is written in pastry: both make kannoli, but Malta's uses sheep's milk ricotta (milder, creamier). Fill only at serving — the crispy shell softens within minutes.

drinks.name: Kinnie
instructions: Pour over ice
Garnish with orange
drinks.description: Malta's signature bitter orange soft drink.

drinks.name: Ġellewża Wine
instructions: Serve at room temperature
Pair with rabbit stew
drinks.description: Indigenous Maltese red wine grape — fruity and earthy.

drinks.name: Kinnie (Bittersweet Orange Soda)
ingredients: Kinnie (Malta's national soft drink — commercially produced)
Optional: gin (the Kinnie G&T is popular)
instructions: Kinnie is Malta's national non-alcoholic beverage — produced since 1952
Made with bitter oranges and aromatic herbs — the recipe is a closely guarded secret
The flavor: bittersweet orange with herbal undertones — between Aperol and bitter lemon
Serve over ice with an orange slice
The Kinnie G&T: mix with gin — a very popular Maltese sundowner
It was created to give Malta a national drink identity
Now it defines Maltese refreshment — ordered everywhere in summer
The bittersweet flavor is polarizing for visitors but deeply nostalgic for Maltese people
Kinnie is also used in desserts and cocktails
Malta without Kinnie is like France without Pastis
drinks.description: Malta's national soda — a bittersweet orange-and-herb drink produced since 1952, Malta's answer to having its own national soft drink identity. The exact formula is secret; the flavor sits between bitter lemon and Aperol. Polarizing for visitors, deeply nostalgic for Maltese people. Also paired with gin as the Maltese G&T.
